passage:
Holi morning: Pradeep covers his eyes with coloured hands in the open courtyard. "Can't see me!" he giggles. Jyoti didi laughs and sprinkles pink on his head.
Two days later: At Nani's house, he hides his face in the curtain, feet sticking out. "Where's Pradeep?" Nani asks, playing along.
Next week: Pradeep shows Mumma his new drawing, holding it facing himself. "Look, Mumma!" Mumma gently turns it round. "Now I can see!" Pradeep looks puzzled, then turns it back.

qa.q: What did Pradeep hide his face in at Nani's house?
qa.a: The curtain, with his feet sticking out.

qa.q: Why does Pradeep think no one can see him?
qa.a: He is happy and sure that if he can't see others, they can't see him; he can't yet imagine how things look from someone else's place.

qa.q: How can adults respond to this stage?
qa.a: Play along gently, as Nani does, and show him other views kindly, as Mumma does by turning the drawing round, without teasing.

qa.q: What is it like for Jyoti didi when Pradeep hides in the open?
qa.a: She finds it funny and sweet, and joins the fun by sprinkling pink on his head.

grounding: A toddler believes covering his eyes hides him and holds a drawing facing himself.

passage: In their Delhi flat, little Lokesh squeezed behind the sofa with only his head hidden and his bottom in the air. "No see me!" he called. His cousin Rehana spotted him at once. "I see you! Your pants are red!" Lokesh stayed still, sure he was invisible. Rehana crept over and tickled his foot. He squealed, astonished. "How?" Mamu laughed and crouched down. "Your eyes were hiding, not your feet." Lokesh covered his eyes again.

qa.q: What colour were Lokesh's pants?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: Why is Lokesh astonished when Rehana tickles his foot?
qa.a: He was sure he was invisible because his own head was hidden, so being found surprises him; he can't yet imagine how he looks from outside.

qa.q: How does Mamu help?
qa.a: He crouches down and explains simply that Lokesh's eyes were hiding, not his feet, without teasing.

qa.q: How does Rehana see the game?
qa.a: Rehana, being older, sees Lokesh clearly and enjoys finding him, amused that he thinks he is hidden.

grounding: A toddler hides only his head and believes no one can see him.

passage:
"Didi, see! Doggy!" Sahil held up the book, the picture facing his own nose.
"I can only see the back, Sahil," said Devika.
"Doggy! Big doggy!"
"Turn it round?"
Sahil looked at the page, then at Devika. "Doggy here!" He tapped the picture.
Amma laughed from the kitchen. "He thinks you see what he sees."
Devika went round and sat beside him. "Oh! A big brown doggy!"
Sahil beamed. "Yes!"

qa.q: What was in Sahil's picture?
qa.a: A big brown doggy.

qa.q: Why does Sahil keep the book facing himself?
qa.a: He is excited to share and thinks Devika sees exactly what he sees; he can't yet imagine her view from the other side.

qa.q: What did Devika do that worked?
qa.a: Instead of arguing, she sat beside him to see from his side and joined in, which pleased him.

qa.q: What is it like for Devika at first?
qa.a: She is a little puzzled, maybe frustrated, seeing only the back of the book.

grounding: A toddler holds a picture facing himself, assuming his sister sees what he sees.

passage: Note to Hrithik's class teacher, Onam week. At home yesterday Hrithik said, "Jaya did the thing again and it fell and everyone laughed!" and waited for me to be shocked. I didn't know who Jaya was, what fell, or where. When I asked, he looked annoyed, as if I should already know. He also insisted I would love the green jelly, because he loves it. Could you tell me what happened with Jaya? At home I'm helping him start his stories with "At school today..." and say who and where.

qa.q: What did Hrithik insist the parent would love?
qa.a: The green jelly.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik look annoyed when asked questions?
qa.a: He felt frustrated, assuming the parent already knew what he had seen at school, as if everyone shared his view.

qa.q: What is the parent doing to help?
qa.a: Asking the teacher what happened, and teaching him to start with "At school today..." and say who and where.

qa.q: How might the parent feel hearing a half-story?
qa.a: Puzzled and a bit lost, trying to follow a story with no who, what or where.

grounding: A preschooler assumes his parent knows what he saw at school and that others like what he likes.

passage: On a foggy winter evening in the village, Abhinav burst into the courtyard. "Dada! The goat did it again, and Yogesh cried, and then the bell!" Dada put down his newspaper. "Which goat, beta? Which bell?" Abhinav stamped his foot. "THE goat! You know!" Dada didn't know; he hadn't been at school. Abhinav was sure everyone had seen what he saw. Then he offered Dada a sticky jaggery sweet from his pocket. "You love these, na? I love them." Dada smiled. "Start from the beginning. Where were you?"

qa.q: What did Abhinav offer Dada?
qa.a: A sticky jaggery sweet from his pocket.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav stamp when Dada asked which goat?
qa.a: He felt frustrated because he assumed Dada already knew, as if everyone had seen what he saw.

qa.q: What helped Dada understand?
qa.a: Asking Abhinav to start from the beginning and say where he was.

qa.q: How does Dada experience the half-story?
qa.a: Dada is puzzled but patient, smiling and asking questions to fill in the gaps.

grounding: A preschooler tells a half-story assuming his grandfather saw it too, and assumes others love what he loves.

passage: On the way home from nursery one autumn afternoon, Diego kicked through the leaves in the London park. "Freya had the red one and then it broke and it was so sad," he said. His mum waited. "The red what, love?" "The RED one!" Diego frowned; surely she knew. At home he gave Mum his half-eaten pumpkin biscuit. "You're sad too, so you have it." Mum wasn't sad at all, but she took it. "Thank you. Was it Freya's red crayon?" Diego nodded hard, relieved.

qa.q: What did Diego give his mum?
qa.a: His half-eaten pumpkin biscuit.

qa.q: Why did Diego give his mum the biscuit?
qa.a: He felt sad about the broken red thing and assumed his mum felt sad too, as if everyone shares his feelings.

qa.q: How did Mum help?
qa.a: She stayed patient, took the biscuit kindly, and asked a specific guess until he could confirm it.

qa.q: How might Mum feel during the walk?
qa.a: Curious and a little puzzled, trying to work out a story that assumed she had been there.

grounding: A preschooler tells half-stories as if his mother saw them and thinks she shares his feelings.

passage: Class note, Christmas week. Rashmi grabbed the angel costume from Ritu and ran. Ritu cried. I asked Rashmi, "Look at Ritu's face. What do you think she's feeling?" Rashmi said, "Happy?" We looked at our feelings chart together, and she pointed to "sad". Then we played a quick pretend game with two dolls, one taking a toy from the other. Rashmi made the doll say, "That's mine, I'm sad!" She went and gave the costume back. Tomorrow we will act out sharing again.

qa.q: What did Rashmi grab from Ritu?
qa.a: The angel costume.

qa.q: What did Rashmi first think Ritu was feeling, and why?
qa.a: Rashmi guessed "happy", because she herself was happy with the costume and couldn't yet see Ritu's side; the chart helped her see the sadness.

qa.q: Which tools did the teacher use?
qa.a: Asking about Ritu's face, a feelings chart, and pretend play with dolls, so Rashmi could see the other side.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel when the costume comes back?
qa.a: Relieved and comforted, though perhaps still a little wary.

grounding: A caregiver uses questions, a feelings chart and pretend play to help a preschooler see another child's feelings.

passage: On Lohri evening in the village, Himani wouldn't let her younger cousin Tushar near the bonfire popcorn. "Mine!" Dadi sat both children on her charpai. "Himani, if Tushar had all the popcorn, how would your tummy feel?" Himani thought. "Empty. Angry." "And how is Tushar's tummy now?" Himani peeked at him; his lip was wobbling. Dadi picked up two small clay cups. "Let's pretend this cup is Himani and this one is Tushar. What does Tushar-cup say?" Himani made the cup squeak, "I want some too!" Then she tipped popcorn into his hands.

qa.q: What wouldn't Himani let Tushar near?
qa.a: The bonfire popcorn.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when she imagined Tushar having all the popcorn?
qa.a: She said her tummy would feel empty and angry, which helped her connect to how Tushar felt.

qa.q: How did Dadi build Himani's perspective taking?
qa.a: She asked how Himani would feel in Tushar's place and used two clay cups for pretend play, so Himani voiced Tushar's view.

qa.q: What might Tushar feel when Himani shares?
qa.a: He is likely happy and relieved after feeling left out.

grounding: A grandmother uses questions and pretend play with cups to help a preschooler take another child's view.

passage: On Three Kings morning in Seville, Alejandro tore open his new train and wouldn't let his little brother Pablo touch it. Pablo sobbed. Papá knelt down with the picture book they had been reading. "Look, here's the bear who wouldn't share. How does the little bear feel?" Alejandro pointed. "Sad. Crying." "Who does he look like?" Alejandro looked at Pablo. "Pablo." Papá said gently, "From where Pablo sits, the train is shiny and far away." Alejandro pushed one carriage over. "This one's yours."

qa.q: What did Alejandro get on Three Kings morning?
qa.a: A new train.

qa.q: What did Alejandro feel when he saw that the sad bear looked like Pablo?
qa.a: He seemed to feel a pang of sympathy, linking the bear's sadness to his brother's.

qa.q: How did Papá help Alejandro see Pablo's side?
qa.a: He used a picture book, asked how the little bear felt, and said aloud how things looked from where Pablo sat.

qa.q: How might Pablo feel when he gets a carriage?
qa.a: He is probably comforted and happy to be included.

grounding: A parent uses a picture book and modelled words to help a preschooler see his brother's view.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Diwali holidays, day two. At the rangoli competition, Zainab wanted to use blue and I wanted orange. I said, "Okay, you like blue, I like orange, that's allowed." I felt very grown-up! Then her team won the prize and ours didn't, and I said she cheated. I KNEW she didn't. I just felt so bad inside that it came out. Mumma said, "You understood she likes blue. Can you also understand she's happy, even if you're sad?" I'm trying. It's harder when I'm upset. Tomorrow I'll say sorry to Zainab.
Baljeet

qa.q: What colour did Zainab want to use?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet say Zainab cheated?
qa.a: Baljeet felt so bad and disappointed about losing that the feeling came out as an accusation, even while knowing she hadn't cheated.

qa.q: What is Baljeet planning, and why is it right?
qa.a: To say sorry to Zainab tomorrow, owning the unfair words said while upset.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel being called a cheat?
qa.a: She would likely feel hurt and confused, especially on a day she was happy about winning.

grounding: A child understands a friend can want different things, but struggles to hold that view when upset.

passage: On Sankranti morning in the village, Divyansh and his friend Elizabeth flew kites from the flat roof. "You want the high wind, I want the low," Divyansh said, proud he had noticed. "Different wants." Then Elizabeth's kite cut his string, and his red kite drifted away over the fields. His face went hot. "You did that on purpose! You wanted my kite gone!" Elizabeth stared. "I didn't even see it." Somewhere inside, Divyansh knew she was telling the truth. But the angry feeling was so big that it drowned out the knowing. He stomped downstairs, then stopped on the last step.

qa.q: What colour was Divyansh's kite?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh accuse Elizabeth though part of him knew she was honest?
qa.a: He felt hot, angry and upset about losing his kite, and the big feeling drowned out his understanding that she had her own view.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do next?
qa.a: Take a breath on the step, go back and say he knows she didn't mean it, and perhaps fly a kite together.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel when accused?
qa.a: Shocked and hurt, since she hadn't even seen his kite.

grounding: A child who understands friends want different things still struggles to see a friend's view when he is upset.

passage: During the summer holidays in Guadalajara, Alejandro hid Sofia's ball in the laundry basket while she was inside. "She'll look in the garden," he told his cousin, grinning. "Because she doesn't know I moved it." He was proud of that thought. But when Sofia came out and looked straight in the basket, he shouted, "You peeked! You knew!" Sofia shrugged. "It's always there." Alejandro's cheeks burned. He wanted to win so much that he couldn't believe she had simply guessed. Later, calmer, he admitted, "Maybe you just thought of it."

qa.q: Where did Alejandro hide Sofia's ball?
qa.a: In the laundry basket.

qa.q: Why did Alejandro accuse Sofia of peeking?
qa.a: He wanted to win so badly that frustration and embarrassment stopped him believing she had simply guessed.

qa.q: What could help Alejandro in games like this?
qa.a: Pausing when his cheeks start burning, and reminding himself that others have their own reasons, like "it's always there".

qa.q: How does Sofia see the moment?
qa.a: She seems calm, even puzzled, since for her the basket was simply the obvious place.

grounding: A child understands a friend has different knowledge, but struggles when the wish to win takes over.

passage: Naveen spent twenty minutes at the bathroom mirror of their Chennai flat, staring at the pimple on his chin. At the school annual day, he was sure every head in the hall turned toward it. He kept his hand over his face during the prize list. Afterwards his friend Harish slapped his back. "Why were you hiding? Nobody's looking at you, machan. They're looking at their own phones." Naveen didn't believe him. That night he typed in his notes: "No one understands. Nobody has ever felt this stupid." The next morning, his older cousin, visiting from Bengaluru, laughed at breakfast about her own "volcano chin" at sixteen. Naveen looked up, surprised.

qa.q: Where did Naveen spend twenty minutes?
qa.a: At the bathroom mirror of their Chennai flat.

qa.q: Why did Naveen keep his hand over his face during the prize list?
qa.a: He felt self-conscious and embarrassed, sure every head in the hall was turned toward his pimple.

qa.q: What could help Naveen feel less alone?
qa.a: Hearing stories like his cousin's and talking with friends, which show that others have felt exactly the same.

qa.q: How does Harish see the situation?
qa.a: Harish thinks nobody was looking and finds the hiding a bit funny, not realising how exposed Naveen feels.

grounding: A teenager feels everyone is watching him and that no one has ever felt this way, until a cousin shares the same experience.

passage:
"You don't get it, Varun bhaiya. Nobody gets it."
"Try me."
"She told everyone she likes someone else. In the canteen. Everyone was staring at me."
"Everyone?"
"The whole canteen. I could feel it."
"Hmm. Were they staring, or eating?"
"...Eating, maybe. But it felt like everyone."
"Okay."
"And nobody has ever felt like this. It's like my chest is empty."
"In Class 11, a girl returned my letter with the spelling corrected."
"What? You?"
"Red pen. I didn't leave my room for a whole weekend."
Tarun laughed despite himself. "Seriously?"
"Seriously. So maybe somebody has felt it."

qa.q: What did the girl do with Varun's letter in Class 11?
qa.a: She returned it with the spelling corrected in red pen.

qa.q: Why does Tarun say nobody has ever felt like this?
qa.a: He feels hurt and alone, so his heartbreak seems unique, and he feels exposed, as if the whole canteen was staring.

qa.q: What did Varun do that helped?
qa.a: He listened, gently questioned "everyone", and shared his own similar story so Tarun felt less alone.

qa.q: What might Varun feel hearing his brother's hurt?
qa.a: Varun probably feels tender and protective, remembering his own embarrassing heartbreak.

grounding: A teenager feels his heartbreak is unique and that everyone is watching him, until his brother shares a similar story.

passage: When I was fifteen, I was sure I was the only person in history who felt like a stranger in my own family. I also believed that every time I walked into the gurdwara, the whole sangat noticed my new haircut and judged me. I wrote long, dramatic poems about it. Then I went to a summer theatre camp, and on the second night Rajni, the camp leader, asked us to write one secret feeling on a slip of paper. She read them out without names. Five slips said, "Nobody at home understands me." Three said, "I feel like everyone is watching me." I sat there stunned. My poem was still mine, but I wasn't alone in it. I'm Baljeet, and I still write, just less dramatically.

qa.q: How many slips said "Nobody at home understands me"?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when the slips were read out?
qa.a: Stunned, and then less alone: the feeling was still personal, but others shared it.

qa.q: What made the difference for Baljeet?
qa.a: Meeting other teenagers at camp and hearing their anonymous feelings, which showed the experience was common.

qa.q: What might Rajni have hoped the slip exercise would do?
qa.a: Help the campers see they weren't alone, gently widening their view without dismissing their feelings.

grounding: A teenager believed those feelings were unique and that everyone was watching, until meeting others at camp showed otherwise.

passage:
Monday: Rekha comes home from school and announces that her life is "literally the worst in the world" because she wore the wrong shoes for the class photo. Her mother, Zeenat, bites back "some children have no shoes" and listens instead. "That sounds so embarrassing."
Thursday: Rekha is still talking about the shoes. Zeenat asks, "Did anyone else have a photo problem?" Rekha thinks. "Actually, the girl next to me blinked." "How did she feel?" "Terrible, I think."
The next Sunday: Looking at the printed class photo together, Rekha laughs. "You can't even see my shoes. And her blink is kind of cute." Zeenat smiles and says nothing, pleased.

qa.q: What went wrong in the class photo, according to Rekha?
qa.a: She wore the wrong shoes.

qa.q: What might Zeenat be feeling when she bites back her comment?
qa.a: She is probably tempted to feel impatient, but chooses patience and empathy, seeing this self-focus as a normal stage.

qa.q: How did Zeenat widen Rekha's view over time?
qa.a: She first listened and agreed it sounded embarrassing, then asked whether anyone else had a photo problem, letting Rekha notice another girl's feelings.

qa.q: How does Rekha feel about the photo by Sunday?
qa.a: She feels lighter and amused, seeing that her shoes don't show and even finding the other girl's blink cute.

grounding: A mother treats her teenager's self-focus as a normal stage, listens without dismissing, and gently widens her view over a week.

passage: Avni, you're new to teaching teenagers, so here's something from when my son Jugraj was fifteen. Every evening he said nobody at school had ever suffered like him, and that everyone laughed when he walked in. My first instinct was to say, "Stop the drama, nobody's looking at you." Your Gurpreet aunty bit her tongue, thank God. I just listened. After a few weeks, I asked whether his friend Manpreet ever felt left out. He thought for a long time. "Yes, actually. At lunch." Slowly, month by month, he started noticing others. By seventeen he was the one sitting with the new boy. Patience, beta. The world gets bigger for them if we don't slam the door.

qa.q: Who did Jugraj sit with by seventeen?
qa.a: The new boy.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet's first instinct, and what did she feel?
qa.a: To say "Stop the drama"; she likely felt impatient and frustrated, but chose to listen instead.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the difference?
qa.a: Biting her tongue and listening, then later asking about his friend's feelings, which widened his view gradually.

qa.q: How might Jugraj have felt if she had said "Stop the drama"?
qa.a: Dismissed and more alone, probably shutting down instead of slowly noticing others.

grounding: An elder recalls treating her teenage son's self-focus as a normal stage, listening and slowly widening his view.

passage: It was the day before the annual exams, the staff room was chaos, and Siddharth sir had forty papers to check. Then Pallavi appeared at the door, eyes red. "I can't read the news at assembly tomorrow. Everyone will stare at me. Nobody has ever been this nervous." Siddharth felt the urge to say, "Not now, Pallavi." Instead he pushed the papers aside. "That sounds really hard. Sit." He listened for five minutes. Then he asked, "Remember who read the news last week?" "The boy from 9C." "How was he?" "His voice shook the whole time." "Did you laugh?" "No. I felt bad for him." Pallavi paused. "Oh." The next day she read, her voice shaking a little, and nobody laughed.

qa.q: What did Pallavi say she couldn't do tomorrow?
qa.a: Read the news at assembly.

qa.q: What did Siddharth feel when Pallavi appeared?
qa.a: He felt the urge to say "Not now", stressed with forty papers, but chose patience.

qa.q: How did Siddharth widen Pallavi's view?
qa.a: He listened first, then asked about last week's reader and how she felt about his shaky voice, letting her see that others weren't judging her.

qa.q: How does Pallavi's view change?
qa.a: She realises she felt sympathy, not scorn, for the last reader, so others will probably feel the same about her.

grounding: A teacher treats a teenager's sense that everyone is watching as normal, listens despite pressure, and gently widens her view.

passage:
"Jagdish, did you drop Nani's blue cup?"
"No."
"It has a crack now. See?"
"It was always like that."
"Was it? It was fine this morning, before the Diwali cleaning."
"It was always cracked. And I didn't spill anything."
His mother, Anjali, looked at the puddle of milk by his feet, then at his wet socks.
"Jagdish, you're not in trouble. I just want to know."
Jagdish stared at the floor. "It jumped," he whispered.
Anjali knelt. "Cups do jump sometimes. Help me wipe it?"
He nodded, holding the cloth tight.

qa.q: Whose cup was it?
qa.a: Nani's blue cup.

qa.q: Why does Jagdish insist the cup was always cracked?
qa.a: He is scared of getting into trouble, so saying it didn't happen feels safer than the truth.

qa.q: What helped Jagdish admit it?
qa.a: His mother saying he was not in trouble, and kneeling to help him wipe it up.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel seeing the milk and the wet socks?
qa.a: She probably feels a mix of amusement and tenderness, seeing his fear clearly.

grounding: A preschooler insists a cracked cup was never cracked because fear of trouble outweighs the wish to be accurate.

passage: Class note, monsoon week. During painting, the water pot tipped over Salma's drawing. Pranav was holding the brush right beside it, paint dripping from his sleeve. When I asked what happened, he said firmly, "Nothing spilled." Then: "It was already wet." He looked scared, shoulders up. I told him accidents happen and nobody would be cross. After a minute he said, very softly, "My elbow bumped it." Salma said it was okay. We dried the drawing on the window together. I will mention the day to his parents, gently.

qa.q: Whose drawing got wet?
qa.a: Salma's drawing.

qa.q: Why did Pranav say "Nothing spilled"?
qa.a: He was scared of trouble, shoulders up, so denying it felt safer than admitting the bump.

qa.q: What did the teacher do right?
qa.a: Told him accidents happen and nobody would be cross, then waited, so he could admit it.

qa.q: How might Salma feel about her wet drawing?
qa.a: She was probably upset at first, but forgiving once Pranav admitted it and they dried it together.

grounding: A preschooler denies a spill that clearly happened because fear of trouble is stronger than the wish to be accurate.

passage: On the morning of Eid in their village, Ayesha's elder brother Vishal found his new clay money pot cracked on the shelf. "Ayesha, did you touch it?" "No!" said Ayesha, hands behind her back. "It's not even broken. See? It's fine." A long crack ran down its side. "And I didn't drop it," she added, though nobody had said she dropped it. Ammi came over and sat on the step. "If it cracked, nobody will shout today. It's Eid." Ayesha's lip shook. "I only picked it up. It slipped." Vishal sighed, then laughed. "We'll tie it with string."

qa.q: What did Vishal find cracked?
qa.a: His new clay money pot.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha say the pot wasn't even broken?
qa.a: She was frightened of being in trouble, so pretending the crack wasn't there felt safer.

qa.q: What helped Ayesha tell the truth?
qa.a: Ammi sitting beside her and promising nobody would shout, which made it safe to admit.

qa.q: How does Vishal react once she admits it?
qa.a: He sighs, then laughs, choosing to fix the pot with string rather than stay angry.

grounding: A child insists a cracked pot is fine and that she didn't drop it, because fear of trouble outweighs accuracy.

passage: The week before Diwali, the sugar mill in their small town let Zubin's father go. At dinner, Papa explained it quietly. Zubin nodded, said, "It's fine, you'll find another one," and asked for more rice. After that he never asked about it again. When his sister Lavanya mentioned it, he said, "Everything is FINE," and left the room. But he lay awake counting the turns of the ceiling fan, and he snapped at the dog for barking and at Lavanya for borrowing his pencil. On Diwali night, Mummy sat on his bed. "You can ask me anything, you know. Not knowing can be scarier." Zubin turned to the wall. After a long time he whispered, "Will we be okay?"

qa.q: Where had Zubin's father worked?
qa.a: At the sugar mill in their small town.

qa.q: Why does Zubin keep saying everything is fine?
qa.a: He is frightened, and not knowing feels safer than facing the worry, so he stops asking; the fear leaks out as sleeplessness and snapping.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with him and said he could ask anything because not knowing can be scarier, which let him voice his real question.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel when Zubin snaps at her?
qa.a: Hurt and confused, since she only borrowed a pencil and may not realise he is scared.

grounding: A child whose father has lost his job insists everything is fine and stops asking, while the worry shows in poor sleep and temper.

passage: In the grey weeks before Christmas in Marseille, Ines's mother lost her job at the bakery. Ines heard it through the kitchen door and decided it didn't count. "Everything's normal," she told her friend Omar at school. "Totally normal." She stopped asking her mother anything about it. But she couldn't fall asleep until midnight, and she shouted at Omar for taking the red marker, then cried in the toilets. Her teacher noticed and called her mother that afternoon. That evening her mother sat on her bed. "I'm looking for new work. You can ask me things." Ines pressed her face into the pillow. "I don't want to know," she said. Then, quietly: "Is it bad?"

qa.q: Where did Ines's mother work?
qa.a: At the bakery.

qa.q: Why did Ines tell Omar everything was totally normal?
qa.a: She was scared, and pretending nothing had changed felt safer than facing the worry.

qa.q: What helped a conversation begin?
qa.a: The teacher noticing and calling her mother that afternoon, and her mother inviting questions at bedtime.

qa.q: How might Omar feel when Ines shouts over the marker?
qa.a: Surprised and hurt, not knowing the shouting comes from her hidden worry.

grounding: A child whose mother has lost her job insists everything is normal and stops asking, while tension leaks out as poor sleep and outbursts.

passage: At the school's summer sports camp, Deepak was usually the loudest boy on the field. This week he was quiet, and then suddenly furious when he dropped a catch, throwing his cap on the ground. Vishal sir, the coach, found him later sitting by the water cooler. "All okay at home?" "Yes. Totally fine," Deepak said too quickly. "Papa's just at home now. Nothing's wrong." He hadn't asked his parents a single question since they told him about the job. "I'm not sleeping much," he added, then looked annoyed with himself. Vishal sir sat beside him. "Sometimes not knowing feels safer. But worries grow in the dark." That evening he called Deepak's mother, and the school counsellor met Deepak the next morning.

qa.q: Where did Vishal sir find Deepak?
qa.a: Sitting by the water cooler.

qa.q: Why did Deepak say "totally fine" so quickly?
qa.a: He was worried and scared about his father's job, and denying it felt safer than facing it, though the tension showed in anger and poor sleep.

passage: The parent-teacher meeting was in two hours, and Vandana still hadn't told anyone about the 31 out of 80 in maths. For three days she had said, "Results aren't out yet," and hidden the sheet in her geography book. Now rain was pouring, the bus was late, and her stomach hurt. At the stop, her friend Ritu asked, "What's wrong?" Vandana took a breath and said it aloud for the first time. "I got 31 in maths." Her voice cracked, but the world didn't end. Ritu just nodded. "Okay. That's a fact. What now?" Together they wrote three lines on the back of the sheet: tell Mumma before the meeting, ask for the tuition timetable, redo chapter four. Vandana called home from the bus.

qa.q: What did Vandana score in maths?
qa.a: 31 out of 80.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel saying the result aloud?
qa.a: Scared, her voice cracking, and then a little relieved that the world didn't end.

qa.q: What steps did Vandana take after telling Ritu?
qa.a: She wrote a three-line plan (tell Mumma before the meeting, ask for the tuition timetable, redo chapter four) and called home from the bus.

qa.q: How might Mumma have felt if she had first heard the result at the meeting?
qa.a: Shocked, and perhaps hurt that Vandana had hidden it instead of telling her.

grounding: A teenager who denied a poor result says it aloud to one friend first, then plans and tells a parent.

passage: In their Kolkata flat, Gargi had kept the chemistry pre-board result off the table for a week. "It's fine, the teacher marked strictly," she said to anyone who asked, and changed the subject. But she stopped opening her chemistry book at all. On Sunday her older cousin Minakshi came over to borrow a saree. Alone in the bedroom, Gargi blurted, "I failed chemistry." Just saying it made her eyes sting. Minakshi sat down on the bed. "Okay. Failed by how much?" "Six marks." "Six. That's fixable." Gargi laughed shakily. Saying it once made the next step smaller. That evening she told Baba, and on Monday she asked her teacher which chapters to redo first.

qa.q: By how many marks did Gargi fail?
qa.a: Six marks.

qa.q: What did Gargi feel when she said "I failed chemistry"?
qa.a: Her eyes stung; she felt ashamed and shaky, but saying it once made the next step feel smaller.

qa.q: What did Gargi do after telling Minakshi?
qa.a: She told Baba that evening, and on Monday asked her teacher which chapters to redo first.

qa.q: How does Minakshi respond, and why does it help?
qa.a: Calmly, asking by how much and calling six marks fixable, which makes the fact feel manageable rather than shameful.

grounding: A teenager who brushed off a failed result says it aloud to a cousin first, then tells a parent and plans.

passage: In his Hyderabad hostel room, Harish had a folder on his laptop called "Later". Inside: two mid-term results in red, a fee reminder from the accounts office, and three emails from the student counsellor titled "Checking in". He hadn't opened any of them. "It'll sort itself out," he told his friend Afreen when she asked about the fees. "The scholarship money comes eventually." But each time the laptop chimed, his stomach clenched, and he closed the lid. Then a printed notice appeared under his door: hall tickets would be withheld for unpaid fees, deadline Friday. Harish sat on his bed with the notice for a long time. Afreen found him there. "Let's go to the counsellor. Now. I'll come with you."

qa.q: What was the laptop folder called?
qa.a: "Later".

qa.q: Why did Harish keep closing the laptop?
qa.a: Each chime made his stomach clench with dread, and not looking felt easier than facing the marks and the fees.

qa.q: What is the wise next step, and who should be involved?
qa.a: Going to the counsellor now, as Afreen suggests, and letting the counsellor and accounts office explain the options; ignoring it only made the deadline scarier.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel seeing Harish with the notice?
qa.a: Worried for him, and determined to help, offering to go with him straight away.

grounding: A student ignores falling marks, a fee reminder and counsellor emails until a deadline forces the issue.

grounding: A student avoids his email, attendance and fees because not looking keeps the dread away, until his sister steps in.

passage: Last year I got very good at not looking. My marks were slipping, and a fee instalment was overdue because I had lost a part-time job and hadn't told my parents. The college counsellor, Arohi ma'am, emailed me twice. I archived both without reading them. I told myself it would sort itself out, that next month would be different. It wasn't dread exactly; it was more like a fog I kept walking around. Then the exam form portal locked me out: "Dues pending." Three days to the deadline. That's when I finally opened her emails. She could help arrange a payment plan and study support. I sat in her office that afternoon, embarrassed. I'm Eshaan, and now I open hard emails on the day they arrive.

qa.q: What message did the exam form portal show?
qa.a: "Dues pending."

qa.q: How does Eshaan describe the feeling of not looking?
qa.a: Like a fog Eshaan kept walking around: a dread kept at bay by avoidance, followed by embarrassment when finally facing it.

qa.q: What changed Eshaan's approach, and what habit came from it?
qa.a: The locked portal forced it; Eshaan met the counsellor that afternoon and now opens hard emails the day they arrive.

qa.q: How might Arohi ma'am have felt when Eshaan finally came?
qa.a: Relieved and ready to help, since she had been trying to reach Eshaan with support.

grounding: A student ignores falling marks, unpaid fees and a counsellor's emails until a deadline forces the issue.
